                S.17. COMPUTATIONAL DESIGN AND THE EXISTING COMPARISON
25                                                                                             25

26     The numerical question is whether the learned evaluation block improves the             26

27   economic accuracy or complete work of the NBO map. All comparisons identify the           27

28   economic model, feasible actions, evaluation target, selected policy, final payoff law,   28

29   and work boundaries. A policy-specific confidence interval conditions on its fitted       29

30   objects. A statement about a training method additionally specifies the distribution      30

31   of training randomness and its sampling uncertainty. An interval containing zero          31

32   establishes neither superiority nor practical equivalence.                                32

                           S.17.2. Accuracy objects and economic scale                       12

13                                                                                           13

14     The original finite-population NBO regret upper bounds are approximately              14

15   0.02097, 0.02847 and 0.03039 in dimensions ten, twenty and fifty. The corresponding     15

16   mean schedule improvements are approximately 0.00147, 0.00135 and 0.00161. The          16

17   regret bounds combine the analytical anchor gap with the measured improvement. 17
18   They are reported as absolute upper bounds, without interpreting them as tight          18

19   high-dimensional HJB errors.                                                            19

20     The independent scalar computation uses a monotone implicit HJB scheme and            20

21   full-box action maximization on four original grids. At initial log capital zero, the   21

22   finest domain-six NBO loss is about 3.44 × 10−6 , compared with 1.16 × 10−4 for         22

23   direct policy optimization. At initial state one, the corresponding losses are about    23

24   1.05 × 10−4 and 5.02 × 10−5 . The ordering is therefore state dependent. These are      24

25   finite-grid losses of Markov feedbacks in the scalar model; the widening experiment     25

26   changes both domain and spatial spacing. The residual, refinement and five-state        26

27   accounts remain in Appendix S.15.                                                       27

28     The balance-sheet profiles and the resource fee in (S.118) are transparent model      28

29   experiments. They are not an empirical calibration. The fee transformation reports      29

30   what administration cost a verified utility gain can support under the specified        30

31   log-felicity resource account. It does not provide an additional independent source     31

32   of evidence for the critic.                                                             32

       The original time-budget and fixed-work records retain fitting clocks, simu-

     aries.

     object before its confirmatory evaluation. It must charge failed checks and retain

18                                                                                              18
       The continuation-learning comparison and the finite-observation exercise ad-
19                                                                                              19
     dress separate questions in the capital economy. The former assesses continuation
20                                                                                              20
     evaluation and feasible improvement under its stated volatility parameters and
21                                                                                              21

                                 S.18.1. The capital experiment
26                                                                                              26

27     The experiment uses the capital state equation and objective in (S.99)–(S.100),          27

28   in dimensions ten and fifty. It changes the volatility parameters to σI = 0.6 and          28

29   σC = 0.3; the remaining primitives are T = 1, ρ = 0.04, a = 0.10, κ = 0.15, ζ = 0.2,       29

30   χ = 0.03, and [m, M] = [0.02, 2]. The initial population assigns equal mass to nine        30

31   profiles with means −0.5, 0, 0.5 and cross-sectional spreads 0, 0.25, 0.5. The methods     31

32   share the declared radius-0.1 feasible tube, coupling matrix, initial population, and      32
                                 NEURAL BELLMAN OPERATORS                              109

1    payoff evaluator. This is a parameter regime of the same economic model. The             1

2    earlier comparison, scalar study, and protected-observation experiment retain their      2

3    original volatility parameters and their separate evidence records.                      3

4      Training uses a global grid of 64 cells. Its reference policy is the cell-average      4

5    analytical schedule and remains fixed through all three work levels. The cumulative      5

6    occupation samples contain 256, 512, and 1,024 states. Each state comes from an          6

7    independent reference trajectory at a uniformly selected decision node. Postdecision     7

8    inputs are the pre-noise mean and the next decision date. NBO and Raw share four- 8
9    antithetic continuation targets; all member rollouts and all reused labels are counted. 9
10   These sample sizes define increasing information budgets, not equal floating-point       10

11   work across methods.                                                                     11

12     At each stage NBO fits the spatial continuation derivative by full-replay Sobolev      12

13   mean-square loss, with 1,200 Adam updates followed by L-BFGS. The latter has             13

14   nominal iteration and evaluation limits of 300 and 400; the current line search is       14

15   completed and every actual closure call is counted. A separate time component            15

16   then receives 400 value-fitting updates with the spatial component fixed. NBO and        16

17   Raw use the same feasible actor objective and minibatch/update streams, with 200,        17

18   400, and 800 additional actor updates at the three stages. DPO and HJB use 100, 200,     18

19   and 400 additional updates. The minibatch size is 128; the actor, spatial-critic, time- 19
20   component, and HJB learning rates are 0.003, 0.002, 0.003, and 0.002, respectively. 20
21   Model weights and replay continue across stages. These are declared optimization         21

22   procedures; a common sample budget does not make their optimization costs                22

23   identical.                                                                               23

24     Online certification and independent final confirmation both use 2,048 decision        24

25   cells and 8,192 paths per stream. The selected fixed networks are deployed on that       25

26   finer grid. The learned 64-cell continuation derivative is consequently a predictor in   26

27   the fine-grid mechanism assessment, whose error account includes that discrepancy;       27

28   it is not identified with an exact fine-grid or continuous-time costate. The protocol    28

29   and numerical source were frozen before the confirmation experiment. Exploratory         29

30   pilots that selected the design remain distinct from the confirmatory observations.      30

31     The measured process clock begins before a fresh worker is launched and ends           31

32   after its final evidence is durably written. It includes imports, model setup, de- 32
     110

1    terministic constants, fitting, checks, weight reloading, confirmation, and output. 1
2    Dependency installation and artifact extraction precede this clock and are not                 2

3    charged as method execution time.                                                              3

5    the stated software environment, the stream specifies the complete training and           5

6    checking computation. The distribution does not include arbitrary unrecorded              6

                 S.18.4. Simultaneous inference for the finite method distribution
30                                                                                             30

31     Each returned policy receives N fresh confirmation paths. The confirmation bank         31

32   is independent of fitting, validation, and every stopping decision. Methods share         32
                                   NEURAL BELLMAN OPERATORS                                  113

1    initial profiles and innovations within a stream, whereas the confirmation banks               1

2    of distinct streams are independent. A direct contrast is formed on each common                2

3    path. Its common analytical schedule cancels, and its transfer account contains the            3

4    two policy allowances rather than two copies of the schedule allowance, when both              4

5    entries are simulated candidate gains. An analytical fallback has the exact gain zero. 5
6    A comparison with that fallback retains the other candidate’s full schedule-relative           6

7    transfer account; two analytical fallbacks have the exact difference zero.                     7

8      For one registered endpoint, let Xsj be the numerical path statistic, Ysj =                  8

9    max{−Cs , min(Cs , Xsj )}, and let β s enclose the difference between the continuous- 9
10   time endpoint θs and EYsj . Thus β s includes the appropriate diffusion, imple- 10
11   mentation, clipping-tail, and arithmetic accounts. Put C = maxs Cs , n = |S| N,                11

12   β̄ = |S|−1   ∑s β s , and denote the pooled mean and unbiased sample variance by               12

13   Ȳ and vb.                                                                                     13

28   for the new experiment. The historical experiment retains its separately stated confi- 28
29   dence event. Unused checks do not release probability for additional comparisons. 29
30     The practical-equivalence margin is fixed at 10−4 payoff units. For a direct interval        30

31   [ L, U ], material superiority requires L > 10−4 , and practical equivalence requires          31

32   −10−4 < L ≤ U < 10−4 . Statistical superiority, L > 0, is reported separately. An              32
     114

1    interval containing zero does not establish equivalence. Under log flow utility, the       1

2    fixed margin corresponds to a proportional consumption fee 1 − exp{−10−4 /A},              2

3    where A = (1 − e−ρT )/ρ; for the stated primitives this is approximately 1.0201 basis      3

4    points.                                                                                    4

5      Simultaneous stream intervals also enclose the probability that the randomized           5

6    implementation attains a target g. If they are [ Ls , Us ], the corresponding bounds are   6

     No binomial sampling interval is attached to a population that has been enumerated

     in full. Work is likewise reported over all streams, with unattained runs retained in
11                                                                                              11
     the distribution of work to target. A median over successful runs alone is not the

     method’s median.

1                   S.18.7. Absolute accuracy in the original control problem                   1

2                                                                                               2
       Let ν be the declared uniform distribution over the nine initial profiles, and let
3                                                                                               3
     Jν0 denote the analytical schedule’s payoff. The pointwise anchor account in (S.28)
4                                                                                               4
     implies Vν∗ − Jν0 ≤ Bd,ν after averaging over this initial population. The repeated
5                                                                                               5
     worker records concern this same bound. We verify their profiles and component
6                                                                                               6
     weights and retain the maximum of the already averaged upper bounds if their
7                                                                                               7
     final rounding differs.
8                                                                                               8
       For a method m, write J d,m = 16−1 ∑s Jν (πm,s ). On the simultaneous confirmation
9                                                                                               9
     event, its existing gain lower endpoint satisfies J d,m − Jν0 ≥ Ld,m . Consequently,
10                                                                                              10

11                                                                                              11

12                                                                                              12

13                                0 ≤ Vν∗ − J d,m ≤ Bd,ν − Ld,m .                      (S.88)   13

14                                                                                              14

15     The optimum in this expression ranges over the original adapted action-box class. 15
16   The returned methods use the declared common tube, which is a feasible subset. 16
17   The inequality therefore accounts for absolute loss against the original economic          17

18   problem. It does not identify the unobserved loss or require another probability           18

19   allocation.                                                                                19

20     The reported full-class upper bounds range from 0.025971 to 0.038358 payoff              20

21   units. Their ratios to the declared margin range from 259.8 to 383.6. Thus the current     21

22   absolute account gives guarantees at those explicit tolerances. It does not certify        22

23   proximity to the full optimum within the 10−4 margin, even when a relative method          23

24   comparison is resolved.                                                                    24

26   method comparisons. A positive gain lower endpoint establishes improvement                 26

27   on the schedule; a direct comparison resolves a difference between two trained             27

28   methods; and a small right-hand side of (S.88) would establish proximity to the            28

29   full optimum. These implications concern different quantities. The neural HJB              29

                    S.18.9. Independent scalar training and numerical accuracy
13                                                                                                        13

14     The separate scalar study uses the original volatility calibration, (σI , σC ) =                   14

15   (0.15, 0.10), and the same one-state capital economy. Eight independent Howard                       15

16   solves generate full-box and matched-tube policies on all four prespecified grids. 16
17   The policies are then evaluated by actual interpolation-based deployment on 8,192                    17

18   fresh paths at both 1,024 and 2,048 time steps. The analytical schedule and both                     18

19   frozen scalar neural policies use the same initial states and Brownian paths.                        19

20     All 8 classical solves reached the stated stopping criterion, using at most 3 Howard               20

21   updates at each date. Their finite-grid algebraic bounds range from 1.072 × 10−12                    21

22   to 8.938 × 10−12 . The last joint state–time refinement changes the three initial-state              22

23   values by amounts between 1.724 × 10−4 and 3.250 × 10−4 . The subsequent en- 23
24   largement of the domain changes these values by at most 4.441 × 10−16 . Thus the                     24

25   algebraic solve, the training-grid approximation, and the finite-domain approxima- 25
26   tion have separate, observable numerical accounts. The small domain change does                      26

27   not bound the remaining time or spatial discretization error.                                        27

28     At 2,048 deployment steps, the largest-domain classical policy has a mean sched- 28
29   ule gain of 7.819 × 10−4 , compared with 7.412 × 10−4 for NBO and 7.065 × 10−4                       29

30   for DPO. The paired classical advantages are 4.069 × 10−5 (Monte Carlo standard                      30

31   error 6.841 × 10−7 ) against NBO and 7.541 × 10−5 (4.063 × 10−7 ) against DPO. Both                  31

8                                                                                              8
                     S.18.10. Implementation from finite state measurements
9                                                                                              9

10     The implementation question has a direct economic interpretation. A manager             10

11   observes a vector of log capital stocks at specified dates, computes consumption          11

12   rates with the saved network, and holds those rates until the next observation. The       12

13   manager’s input consists of the measured physical state. The finite-observation           13

14   controller does not require a Brownian coordinate or the intervening drift integral. 14
15   Proposition S.20 applies to this controller through a protected parent with the same      15

16   saved weights and inward action guard.                                                    16

17     The experiment verifies that parent afresh at 1,024 and 4,096 decision dates in         17

18   dimensions 10 and 50. It retains the original volatility calibration and the previously   18

19   fixed iteration-80 NBO weights; no outcome in the new observation experiment              19

20   selects a policy. Table S.19 subtracts each deterministic sensing allowance from the      20

21   corresponding parent guarantee. All four parents have positive lower endpoints. 21
22   Six of the twelve finite-observation lower endpoints remain positive. With 4,096          22

23   dates and exact measurements, the continuous-economy gain is at least 0.001050 in         23

24   dimension 10 and 0.001054 in dimension 50. In dimension 10, a measurement error           24

25   of 0.0001 retains a lower gain of 0.000889 at the finer grid.                             25

26     The dependence on measurement precision is economically material. At dimen- 26
27   sion 50, an error of 0.0001 already exceeds the available parent margin under the         27

28   current global network bound, and an error of 0.001 removes a positive guarantee          28

29   in both dimensions. These endpoints give an implementation requirement for the            29

30   specific measured-state rule. They do not infer the sign of its actual gain when the      30

31   allowance is too large. The full intervals, allowance-to-gain ratios, and fresh-process   31

32   costs appear in Tables S.28 and S.29.                                                     32

10                                                                                                            10
                      S.23. DESIGN OF THE REUSABLE CAPITAL DECISION MENU
11                                                                                                            11
          This experiment evaluates the finite Bellman object in (S.1). A current task changes
12                                                                                                            12
     the consumption utility weight w, the coefficient η on squared mean consumption,
13                                                                                                            13
     or the current upper consumption bound u. All future primitives and the feasible
14                                                                                                            14
     future schedule remain fixed within a calibration. The continuation identity in
15                                                                                                            15
     Proposition S.14 therefore holds across tasks. A change to the future horizon, tech-
16                                                                                                            16
     nology, preferences, innovation law, terminal dispersion cost, or schedule defines a
17                                                                                                            17
     different continuation and requires a different cache or fitted object.
18                                                                                                            18

19                                                                                                            19
                             S.23.1. Calibrations and the query population
20                                                                                                            20

21        Table S.31 records all four calibrations. The drift uses the original fixed dense                   21

22   coupling matrix in dimensions ten and fifty, with f (y) = κ tanh( By). Productivity                      22

23   is 0.1, discounting is 0.04, the future consumption penalty coefficient is 0.2, and                      23

24   the original consumption interval is [0.02, 2]. The terminal penalty is proportional                     24

25   to cross-sector dispersion. The period weights, feasible reference schedule, drift                       25

26   constant, innovation amplitudes, and terminal coefficients are stored before fitting. 26
27   Their binary64 values, together with the stored states and coupling matrices, are the                    27

28   exact real coefficients of the finite economic problem under study. The continuous- 28
29   diffusion primitives motivate these coefficients; they do not make the coarse finite                     29

30   value an unqualified continuous-time approximation.                                                      30

31        Nine tasks are the Cartesian product w ∈ {0.8, 1, 1.2} and η ∈ {0.1, 0.2, 0.4} with                 31

32   u = 2. The other three are (w, η, u) = (0.9, 0.3, 0.6), (1.1, 0.15, 0.8), and (1, 0.25, 1). 32
                                      NEURAL BELLMAN OPERATORS                                            151

9                                                                                                               9
     streams. Original retains the original low-volatility primitive anchor. Quarterly was used in one
10   disclosed exploratory five-method pilot; Long and Intermediate had no method-development or                10

11   outcome pilot. Long increases calendar time and the length of a period relative to Quarterly while         11

12   retaining eight periods.                                                                                   12

13                                                                                                              13

14   Every task retains the lower bound 0.02. The first nine appeared in the disclosed                          14

15   pilot; the three tighter-cap tasks did not. Each dimension has thirty-two stored                           15

16   states crossed with all twelve tasks. The inferential population is the uniform finite                     16

17   collection of these 384 queries and the sixteen declared streams, separately in each                       17

18   calibration and dimension. No query, stream, task, or work stage is removed because                        18

19   of its realized performance. Training inputs, method failures, completed prefixes,                         19

20   and feasible reference fallbacks remain recorded.                                                          20

22                                                                                                              22
                                      S.23.2. Five reusable procedures
23                                                                                                              23

24     The NBO scalar critic and the vector costate predictor both have width thirty-two. 24
25   At each work stage they share the same replay states, uniform feasible training                            25

26   actions, postdecision arguments, and four-path antithetic continuation labels. The                         26

27   scalar critic fits gradients of one differentiable continuation; an intercept fits its                     27

28   level using the value labels. The vector predictor fits costate components without                         28

29   the restriction that they be the gradient of a scalar. These procedures consequently                       29

30   share observations while using different fitted function classes and optimization                          30

31   objectives. Their economic contrast does not by itself isolate a single statistical                        31

32   mechanism.                                                                                                 32
     152

1      The materialized Raw procedure stores costate labels at the reference current           1

2    consumption. Its task-conditioned actor maximizes the exact current reward and the        2

3    corresponding linearized continuation in the action. Direct policy optimization also      3

4    uses a task-conditioned actor, but retains innovations and recomputes the nonlinear       4

5    future payoff at each proposed postdecision argument. Both actors have width              5

6    thirty-two. Query-level Raw instead optimizes each of the 384 task-state decisions        6

7    directly against a sample-average continuation. Its innovation cache grows from           7

8    four to sixteen to sixty-four antithetic paths, and its previous action initializes the   8

9    next stage. Retaining an innovation does not eliminate the state-recursion work           9

10   required by a new argument. All five methods follow the same cache-validity rule. 10
11     For the fitted procedures, the cumulative replay budgets are 128, 512, and 2,048        11

12   states. Each field stage has 1,200 Adam updates with learning rate 0.003, followed        12

13   by L-BFGS with at most 300 iterations and 400 function evaluations. Each actor stage      13

14   has 1,200 Adam updates with learning rate 0.003 and batch size 128. Query opti- 14
15   mization uses 180 Adam updates with learning rate 0.06. NBO and sample-average            15

16   Raw then apply L-BFGS to their scalar objective, with at most sixty iterations and        16

17   ninety evaluations. The vector costate procedure retains its 180 gradient-driven ac- 17
18   tion updates; it has no additional scalar-objective L-BFGS stage. All three completed     18

19   stages are assessed. The final payoff bank is inaccessible to fitting and cannot select   19

20   a method, checkpoint, work stage, query, or replacement stream.                           20

21                                                                                             21

22                                                                                             22

23                                                                                             23
                   S.23.3. Independent payoff and scalar-accuracy statements
24                                                                                             24

25     There are 4 × 2 × 16 = 128 trials, 640 method processes, and 1,920 stage candi- 25
26   dates. Conditional on these fitted objects, each task-state query has 512 independent     26

27   antithetic confirmation pairs. Common innovations pair the method contrasts. 27
28   Proposition S.16 supplies the query-conditional range after removing known ana- 28
29   lytic centers. The numerical account also retains the fixed Gaussian truncation and       29

30   arithmetic allowances. The primary family allocates error 0.018 across all 216 events:    30

31   120 method-versus-reference gains and 96 direct NBO-versus-comparator contrasts. 31
32   Thus every comparator has twenty-four direct statements across all calibrations,          32
                                   NEURAL BELLMAN OPERATORS                                    153

1    dimensions, and stages. There are no additional per-stream confidence events or                  1

2    continuation-risk estimates.                                                                     2

3      The economic superiority margin is 10−4 . A protected lower contrast above zero                3

4    establishes a positive difference; material superiority requires the lower contrast              4

5    to reach 10−4 . Equivalence requires the complete interval to lie in [−10−4 , 10−4 ]. 5
6    Positive differences and equivalence can therefore both be established for the same              6

7    comparison. These categories are reported separately. Training loss and an observed              7

8    economic payoff gain do not establish a reduction in independent critic mean- 8
9    squared error.                                                                                   9

10     The separate scalar family allocates error 0.002 across 128 statements. For the                10

11   central task (w, η, u) = (1, 0.2, 2) and the first stored state (index zero), a successful fit   11

12   selects its candidate using the final NBO critic on 257 fixed grid points in the interval        12

13   consisting of the reference current consumption plus or minus 0.1, intersected                   13

14   with the action box. A failed fit retains the predeclared feasible reference fallback. 14
15   All sectors receive this same scalar action. The independent verifier uses 65,536                15

16   antithetic pairs and the proved derivative and curvature account to cover the entire             16

17   continuous interval, including points between the candidate grid. These bounds                   17

18   concern this restricted finite scalar intervention. They do not bound regret over all            18

19   vector actions, future adapted policies, or the continuous diffusion.                            19

20                                                                                                    20

21                                                                                                    21

22                                                                                                    22
                          S.23.4. Complete work and development history
23                                                                                                    23

24     The final-stage process clock covers startup, imports, input checking, all three               24

25   fitting stages, caches, derivative and optimization work, query deployment, candi- 25
26   date output, and finalization. Earlier-stage clocks combine the executed prefix with             26

27   all measured outer overhead and finalization; they are conservative allocations of               27

28   this run. They are not observations from separate online stopping experiments. The               28

29   independent confirmation process is a shared workload covering all five methods,                 29

30   all three stages, and the scalar assessment. Its full bill is reported separately. Charg- 30
31   ing that bill to each method is an explicit upper allocation, not a measurement of               31

32   five independently executed verification jobs. Timing summaries describe these                   32
     154

1    runs; the confidence family makes no claim about an unseen runtime or optimizer        1

2    distribution.                                                                          2

3       The development archive retains the single exploratory five-method menu pilot, 3
4    its interrupted preliminary attempt, and all twelve fixed-random-feature explo- 4
5
     rations, including their adverse results. Their payoff observations are not confir- 5
     mation observations. The final source fixes new streams, the complete task popu-
6                                                                                           6
     lation, every budget, both margins, failure behavior, power calculations, and all
7                                                                                           7
     inference code before the registered fitting and confirmation. The independent fixed-
8                                                                                           8
     dictionary identity in Proposition S.15 describes a precise conditional statistical
9
     benefit and its approximation cost. It neither identifies the nonlinear fitted network 9
10
     with that projection nor makes the observed five-procedure economic comparison a 10
11   causal decomposition of critic risk.                                                   11

28   share each pair. All three stages and all eight economic-dimension cells contribute to one 216-event     28

29   family with error probability 0.018. Current reward and a known terminal quadratic are removed           29
     before the random residual is bounded. The mean column is the clipped residual estimator plus this
30                                                                                                            30
     known offset. Numerical arithmetic, clipping and the unclipped Gaussian law are included. The
31                                                                                                            31
     materiality margin is 10−4 .

                    S.24. INDEPENDENT CONFIRMATION OF THE ORIGINAL POLICIES                                        23

             S.25. ECONOMIC ROBUSTNESS AND THE STRENGTHENED HJB PROCEDURE
27                                                                                                            27

28     This experiment changes the continuous-diffusion capital economy and trains                            28

29   all procedures anew. It is separate from both the confirmation of 128 previously                         29

30   selected policies and the finite-period continuation menu. Its four economic calibra- 30
31   tions, dimensions ten and fifty, and eight fixed training streams give 64 trials. The                    31

32   report retains all 256 construction processes and 320 deployed policy outputs. All                       32
     174

1    procedures completed without reference-policy fallback. A fresh bank of 8,192 paths                         1

2    on 2,048 cells assesses each output, with common innovations within a trial. The                            2

3    648-event family has allocation α = 0.01 and includes method averages, individual- 3
4    policy endpoints, and the declared direct comparisons. No calibration or stream is                          4

5    selected on its outcome.                                                                                    5

6                                                                                                                6

7                                        S.25.1. Economic variation                                              7

8                                                                                                                8
       Table S.41 gives the complete economic grid. The high calibration retains the
9                                                                                                                9
     original high-volatility diffusion; low changes its diffusion risk. The longer-horizon
10                                                                                                               10
     economy has horizon two years. The joint-stress economy changes coupling, termi-
11                                                                                                               11
     nal dispersion costs, initial heterogeneity, and the actor’s feasible radius together. Its
12                                                                                                               12
     comparison therefore describes that economic design rather than a single-primitive
13                                                                                                               13
     causal effect. These names are local to the continuous economy: in particular, the
14                                                                                                               14
     finite menu’s Long calibration has a four-year horizon and half-year periods.

29                                                                                                               29
                         S.25.2. HJB differentiation, selection, and deployment
30                                                                                                               30

31     The two-layer tanh value network propagates its value, gradient, and covariance- 31
32   contracted Hessian by the chain rule. The diffusion trace is exact for this network in                      32
                                 NEURAL BELLMAN OPERATORS                              175

1    both dimensions, so training uses no random trace estimate. Independent automatic- 1
2    differentiation checks compare both the network derivatives and their parameter          2

3    gradients. The source validation records discrepancies at floating-point precision. 3
4    Stochastic traces with 2, 8, and 32 probes are evaluated only on an untouched            4

5    finite diagnostic bank after selection, for both covariance-Gaussian probes and          5

6    idiosyncratic Rademacher probes with the common-noise term treated exactly.              6

7      Four candidates combine learning rates .0015 and .0005 with either reference           7

8    occupation collocation or an equal mixture of reference occupation and broad             8

9    collocation. Each uses up to 1,200 Adam updates and 150 L-BFGS iterations. Check- 9
10   points are evaluated on independent occupation and broad residual banks; the             10

11   combined residual criterion chooses the candidate and checkpoint. Its prescribed         11

12   residual threshold is .001. Final payoff observations play no role in selection. Every   12

13   candidate, including an unsuccessful or unselected candidate, is charged to the          13

14   procedure.                                                                               14

15     The selected value network yields two retained actions. The greedy action uses         15

16   the explicit first-derivative calculation and a bracketed scalar root solver with New- 16
17   ton updates; the prescribed bisection fallback remains part of the implementation. 17
18   A width-32 actor is separately fitted to these actions. Independent diagnostic states    18

19   record its action difference and Hamiltonian difference from the greedy action. 19
20   These are finite-state diagnostics. They do not establish the economic loss of distil- 20
21   lation, since the protected family does not contain a direct greedy-minus-distilled      21

22   payoff contrast.                                                                         22

23     The diagnostic tables below retain all four configurations in all eight economic       23

24   cells. Their means and ranges use all eight streams in each cell. The complete           24

25   checkpoint histories, time-stratified residuals, selected network identities, root       25

26   counters, and action diagnostics remain in the unchanged machine-readable report. 26
27   A zero terminal discrepancy follows from the specified terminal lift. Residuals on       27

28   finite independent banks and changes between iterates are reported with their            28

29   corresponding scope; they are not uniform PDE residual bounds or errors against          29

30   the unknown optimal value and policy.                                                    30

25     This section concerns the finite continuation economy defined in Section S.1.2. 25
26   All expectations below use its unclipped Gaussian law and its stored economic                                26

27   coefficients. Conditioning on a fitted continuation is different from assuming a                             27

28   fixed feature dictionary before training. The results in this section permit nonlinear                       28

29   fitting, data-dependent features, and actions chosen by the fitted critic, provided                          29

30   the assessment innovations are independent of these choices.                                                 30

14     P ROPOSITION S.25—Action contrasts and economic decisions: Let r j be the known                          14

15   current-reward difference between the two actions. The selector that chooses the first ac- 15
16   tion when r j + p Mj ≥ 0 has loss, relative to the better of these two actions, bounded by                 16
                                                             √
17   | p Mj − c j |. Consequently its average loss is at most R M . An additive error of at most                17

18   η j in maximizing the predicted two-action objective adds η j to the pointwise bound. For a                18

19   finite action catalog with reference contrast c j0 = p Mj0 = 0, an η j -approximate predicted              19

20   maximizer instead has loss at most                                                                         20

21                                                                                                              21
                                              2 max | p Mja − c ja | + η j .
22                                                 a                                                            22

23
     If the catalog risk at query j is ∑ a w ja ( p Mja − c ja )2 and w ja ≥ w > 0 for every action, the        23

24                                                                                                              24
     last bound is at most twice the square root of this risk divided by w, plus η j .
25                                                                                                              25

26     P ROOF : Put v = r j + c j and vb = r j + p Mj . When the selectors based on v and                       26

27   vb agree, the loss is zero. When they disagree, zero lies between v and vb, so the                         27

28   loss |v| is at most |v − vb|. For an approximate choice, the same argument bounds                          28

29   a wrong choice by |v − vb| + η j . Averaging and applying Cauchy–Schwarz proves                            29

30   the risk bound. For a catalog let a∗ maximize the true objective and let b
                                                                              a be the                          30

31   approximate predicted maximizer. Insert the predicted objective at a∗ and b
                                                                               a into                           31

1    is at most the maximum contrast error. Finally, each squared error is at most the                 1

2    weighted risk divided by its weight. This proves every assertion.                      Q.E.D.     2

       The first assertion provides an economic unit for the risk without asserting that
4                                                                                                      4
     risk ordering determines payoff ordering. Such an assertion is false: when the true
5                                                                                                      5
     net contrast is .01, predictions −.01 and .2 have squared errors .0004 and .0361,
6                                                                                                      6

7                                                                                                      7

8                                                                                                      8

9                                                                                                      9
     full adapted diffusion class.

       The implementation takes q j to be a representative of the known terminal
7                                                                                             7

16         S.27. SHARP ACCURACY BOUNDS FROM SIMULTANEOUS PAYOFF CONTRASTS                     16

17                                                                                            17
       Fix a finite nonempty set I of computed procedures, all evaluated on the same
18                                                                                            18
     declared economic population. For each supplied pair ( a, b), let [ L ab , Uab ] be a
19                                                                                            19
     finite interval for Va − Vb . All intervals are assumed to hold on one event E with
20                                                                                            20
     probability at least 1 − α. No independence across intervals is required. Define
21                                                                                            21
                              I
22               U = {v ∈ R : L ab ≤ v a − vb ≤ Uab for every supplied pair}.                 22

23                                                                                            23
     The graph has an edge b → a of length Uab and an edge a → b of length − L ab for
24                                                                                            24
     every supplied pair. It is connected in both directions in the application, because
25                                                                                            25
     every candidate has a comparison with the reference. The convention for the empty
26                                                                                            26
     path is length zero.
27                                                                                            27

28     P ROPOSITION S.29—Exact catalogue closure: Suppose the graph is strongly con- 28
29   nected and contains no negative cycle. Let Dij be its shortest-path lengths. Then U is   29

30   nonempty, Dii = 0, and                                                                   30

31                                                                                            31
                                    sup(v j − vi ) = Dij ,                           (S.96)
32                                   v∈U                                                      32
     188

1                                 inf {max v j − vi } = max(− D ji ),                      (S.97)    1
                                 v∈U     j                j
2                                                                                                    2

3                                sup{max v j − vi } = max Dij .                            (S.98)    3
                                 v∈U     j                j
4                                                                                                    4

5    All three extrema are attained. Normalizing the reference value to zero does not change them.   5

6    On E , these bounds hold simultaneously for every candidate and every pair, including pairs     6

7    not directly compared in the original report.                                                   7

8                                                                                                    8
       P ROOF : Every edge a → b of length w imposes vb − v a ≤ w. Summing along
9                                                                                                    9
     a path and then minimizing yields v j − vi ≤ Dij for every v ∈ U . There are finite
10                                                                                                   10
     shortest paths because the graph is finite, strongly connected, and has no negative
11                                                                                                   11
     cycle. They satisfy the triangle inequality Dib ≤ Dia + Dab and Dii = 0. For fixed i,
12                                                                                                   12
     the vector v+
                 k = Dik satisfies each original edge constraint: if a → b has length w, then
13                                                                                                   13
     Dib ≤ Dia + w. It therefore belongs to U and attains v+    +
                                                           j − vi = Dij simultaneously
14                                                                                                   14
     for all j. This proves (S.96) and (S.98).
15                                                                                                   15
       For the lower bound, reversing the pairwise inequality gives v j − vi ≥ − D ji .
16                                                                                                   16
     The vector v−
                 k = − Dki is also feasible, since the same edge implies Dai ≤ w + Dbi
17                                                                                                   17
     and hence v−     −                                             −     −
                b − v a = Dai − Dbi ≤ w. It simultaneously attains v j − vi = − D ji ,
18                                                                                                   18
     proving (S.97). Both extrema include j = i, so both regret bounds are nonnegative.
19                                                                                                   19
     Subtracting the reference coordinate leaves every difference unchanged. Finally, on
20                                                                                                   20
     E the true payoff vector belongs to U ; all deterministic conclusions therefore hold
21                                                                                                   21
     on that same event.                                                                  Q.E.D.
22                                                                                                   22

23                                                                                                   23
       Sharpness here is relative to the interval-defined uncertainty set. It does not assert
24                                                                                                   24
     that every compatible vector can be generated by the underlying capital model, or
25
     that the original statistical intervals are optimal. A negative cycle makes U empty. 25
26                                                                                                   26
     The implementation stops with an inconsistency diagnostic; it does not delete an
27                                                                                                   27
     unfavorable interval, truncate a negative cycle, or report an accuracy certificate in
28                                                                                                   28
     that case.
29                                                                                                   29

30     C OROLLARY S.30—Selection with an economic tolerance: Let ci ≥ 0 be observed                  30

31   accounting costs and τ ≥ 0. Define Cτ = {i : max j Dij ≤ τ }. When this set is nonempty,        31

32   choose a deterministic tie-broken minimizer bi of ci over Cτ . Then on E , max j Vj − Vb ≤ τ
                                                                                            i        32
                                   NEURAL BELLMAN OPERATORS                                   189

1    and cbi ≤ ck for every k ∈ Cτ . The accuracy assertion remains valid for a tolerance chosen     1

2    after inspecting the intervals, interpreted as a simultaneous assertion for all tolerances. A   2

3    common nonnegative assessment charge preserves the cost ordering.                               3

4                                                                                                    4
       P ROOF : On E all candidate bounds hold at once. Membership of the chosen
5                                                                                                    5
     candidate in Cτ gives its regret bound irrespective of how the index or tolerance
6                                                                                                    6
     was selected. The cost inequality is the definition of the minimizer; addition of the
7                                                                                                    7
     same charge to both sides preserves it. If Cτ is empty, the rule returns no certified
8                                                                                                    8
     candidate.                                                                           Q.E.D.
9                                                                                                    9

10     The corollary gives no assertion about ck for an uncertified candidate with un- 10
11   known true regret below τ. Observed cost is not an expectation over future machines             11

12   or training runs. Selecting after the full computation does not save the work al- 12
13   ready spent computing the competing candidates. In particular, a retrospective                  13

14   least certified prefix allocation is not a measured work-to-target stopping time. 14
15   These distinctions are necessary when the same continuation is amortized across an              15

16   economic decision menu.                                                                         16

17                                                                                                   17

18                    S.27.1. Exact arithmetic and the complete input family                         18

19     The computation reads all 216 original protected intervals: eight economic cells,             19

20   three stages, five gains relative to the common reference, and four direct NBO                  20

21   contrasts at each stage. The stored binary64 endpoints are interpreted as exact                 21

22   rational numbers. Floyd–Warshall updates use only rational addition, ordering,                  22

23   and minima. Final lower endpoints are rounded downward and upper endpoints                      23

24   upward. The reference plus fifteen method-stage candidates are retained in every                24

25   cell, including costly and dominated candidates. All means use the same sixteen                 25

26   streams; no stream is selected on the basis of the analysis. The calculation adds no            26

9         S.31. CONTINUOUS-ECONOMY GUARANTEES FOR NEURAL CAPITAL POLICIES                        9

10                                                                                               10
       The distinction between a nodal certificate and an economic diffusion bound
11                                                                                               11
     is substantive. This section obtains the latter for the original dense, nonlinear
12                                                                                               12
     capital economy, without replacing its primitives, restricting the comparison policy
13                                                                                               13
     class, or extrapolating a sampled residual. The construction uses the curvature
14                                                                                               14
     of consumption utility to control the gain from an arbitrary adapted deviation. A
15                                                                                               15
     neural actor is then confined to a known neighbourhood of a feasible schedule.
16                                                                                               16
     Its approximation class is restricted; the economic optimum against which it is
17                                                                                               17
     assessed is not.

6                                                                                              6
       The bound in Theorem S.9 is a useful starting point, but not a measure of what
7                                                                                              7
     training accomplishes. Every policy in the same tube receives the same allowance,
8
     including a poorly trained policy. We now replace that allowance by an indepen- 8
9                                                                                              9
     dently verified, policy-specific payoff difference. The economic primitives, initial
10
     state, and full adapted comparison class in (S.99)–(S.100) are unchanged. The im- 10
11                                                                                             11
     plementation to which the new bound applies is specified explicitly below. It is not
12                                                                                             12
     identified with continuously observed-state feedback.

1                    S.31.4. Information and the implemented decision rule                     1

2                                                                                              2
       The economic institution is a controller that receives capital observations at
3                                                                                              3
     specified dates, stores an internal state, and holds the selected consumption share
4                                                                                              4
     until the next decision date. Its economic primitive is the original capital diffusion.
5                                                                                              5
     Its internal numerical state need not equal the physical state. When the controller
6                                                                                              6
     uses private randomization, that randomization is part of its specified information
7                                                                                              7
     and is included in the law of the evaluated policy.
8                                                                                              8
       The exact-history representation in Proposition S.18 assumes continuous noise-
9                                                                                              9
     less observation of every capital coordinate, known coefficients and actions, exact
10                                                                                             10
     drift integration, and an independent private Brownian motion. Under those as-
11                                                                                             11
     sumptions the observation history supplies a Brownian representation with the law
12                                                                                             12
     required by the innovation-driven controller. It does not recover the original latent
13                                                                                             13
     null-space shock path by path. Proposition S.19 states why the added independent
14                                                                                             14
     randomization leaves the economic optimum unchanged. These are representation
15                                                                                             15
     results for a randomized history-dependent policy.
16                                                                                             16
       Finite observations require a different implementation account. Proposition S.20
17                                                                                             17
     bounds the difference between the measured-state controller and its specified
18                                                                                             18
     protected parent, retaining sensor error, the internal recurrence, action-map error,
19                                                                                             19
     clipping, and arithmetic. Its allowance belongs to that parent and that time grid.
20                                                                                             20
     The empirical comparison reports it alongside the gain measured for the same
21                                                                                             21
     parent and population; a certificate for a different mesh is not substituted. Complete
22                                                                                             22
     assumptions and proofs are in Appendix S.14.
23                                                                                             23

24                                                                                             24
                   S.31.5. When is state-dependent management worth its fee?
25                                                                                             25

26     To give the policy differences a decision interpretation, consider a proportional       26

27   resource cost τ ∈ [0, 1) for administering a state-dependent consumption rule. Gross      27

28   withdrawals from capital remain mi eYi , and the service absorbs τmi eYi . Household      28

29   consumption is (1 − τ )mi eYi . Production, gross depletion, the gross-withdrawal         29

30   adjustment cost, and terminal capital are unchanged. This is a self-financed resource     30

31   experiment rather than an externally financed utility supplement. It changes the          31

32   specified fee parameter, not the model used to train or benchmark the gross policy. 32
     208
                   R T −ρt
1      Let A T =    0 e    dt. Log felicity gives the exact identity                                      1

2                                                                                                         2

3
                       JPτ ( a) − JP (m0 ) = JP ( a) − JP (m0 ) + A T log(1 − τ ).              (S.118)   3

4                                                                                                         4
     Hence a positive certified improvement L a supports every fee τ satisfying
5                                                                                                         5

6                                        τ < 1 − exp(− L a /A T ).                                        6

7                                                                                                         7
     A negative upper endpoint after the fee rules out an improvement for that candidate
8                                                                                                         8
     under the confidence event; an interval spanning zero is inconclusive. The fee grid is
9                                                                                                         9
     fixed before the final simulation. We do not equate wall-clock cost to a monetary fee
10                                                                                                        10
     or call these deliberately stylized balance sheets a calibrated household population.
11                                                                                                        11
     The experiment instead states precisely which adoption decisions are supported by
12                                                                                                        12
     the verified utility differences.

                       S.32.6. Arithmetic enclosure and its implementation
22                                                                                            22

23     The stored binary64 coefficients and innovation increments define the exact finite     23

24   economy. Floating-point evaluation of a Gaussian generator is not being asserted to      24

25   be exact sampling from a continuous Gaussian economy. The generator is used to           25

26   construct and freeze a finite array; the subsequent scientific statement concerns that   26

27   array with equal masses.                                                                 27

28     The arithmetic module encloses each binary operation by the adjacent repre- 28
29   sentable numbers toward minus and plus infinity. It checks finite values, IEEE           29

30   round-to-nearest behavior and gradual underflow. Products and quotients take             30

31   extrema over endpoint combinations, with divisors bounded away from zero. Squar- 31
32   ing includes zero when the argument interval contains zero. Balanced reductions          32
     214

1    avoid interpreting a non-enclosing ordinary mean as an interval sum. Induction on             1

2    an expression’s operation graph proves inclusion for arithmetic expressions from              2

3    enclosed inputs.                                                                              3

4      The nonlinear enclosure does not assume that a library’s hyperbolic tangent is              4

5    correctly rounded. For 0 ≤ t ≤ 1/2, the exponential is enclosed by its degree-18              5

6    Taylor polynomial and the nonnegative tail bound                                              6

                     S.32.7. Charge monotonicity and the economic tolerance                        24

25     For an interior maximizing action, differentiate Q′θ (y, a∗ (τ )) = 0. Because the          25

26   charge enters the derivative as − A0 τ, the implicit-function identity is Q′′ ∂a∗ /∂τ −       26

27   A0 = 0, proving (29). For the constrained case take τ2 > τ1 and respective optimal            27

28   actions a2 , a1 . Adding their optimality inequalities leaves A0 (τ2 − τ1 )( a2 − a1 ) ≤ 0,   28

29   hence a2 ≤ a1 . Uniqueness follows from strict concavity.                                     29

30     An external grant in the utility account satisfies A0 w log(1 + g) = U exactly when         30

31   g = exp(U/( A0 w)) − 1. This is a monotone normalization of a certified payoff                31

32   loss. The published grant table uses ordinary binary64 evaluation and is explicitly           32
                                NEURAL BELLMAN OPERATORS                             215

1    descriptive; the primary rigorous statement is the outward payoff-loss bound. No       1

2    claim is made that increasing actual endogenous consumption by this amount             2

3    leaves capital, future rewards, or the reference policy unchanged.                     3

                       S.33. PROSPECTIVE EXPERIMENT: COMPLETE RECORD
5                                                                                           5

6      The execution modules and the two finite economic inputs match the original          6

7    implementation freeze. This integrated execution replays that fixed design; it is      7

8    not an additional independent experiment. The original descriptive design file is      8

9    not reconstructed byte for byte. Its replacement documents the unchanged exe- 9
10   cutable choices and is explicitly identified as such. Three fitting/cache streams,     10

11   two dimensions, six query volumes and seven procedures give 252 actual service         11

12   runs. Their task prefixes are deliberately shared, so the 252 runs are not claimed     12

13   to be statistically independent. Synthetic dimension-three algebra checks are not      13

14   economic observations. No registered seed, budget, tolerance or architecture was       14

15   changed using integrated outcomes.                                                     15

16     The stored JSON records contain every selected action, per-task lower curvature      16

17   bound, outward derivative endpoints, individual regret upper bounds, cache in- 17
18   dices, attempted stage, time component, failure status, and post-stop diagnostic. 18
19   The data report generator checks unique identities, the first-success stopping rule,   19

20   positive curvature, arithmetic summaries, and that reported service time covers        20

21   all timed components. These record-consistency checks supplement, rather than          21

22   replace, the mathematical enclosure proof.                                             22

       S.34.0.0.1. Why catalogue averages cannot be substituted. Consider a two-date econ- 19
20                                                                                                          20
     omy with zero first-date rewards. A deviation at the initial state can reach a state
21                                                                                                          21
     with a unit second-date gain that the implemented policy never visits. All local
22                                                                                                          22
     advantages at the implemented policy’s visited states can be zero while the initial
23
     optimality gap equals one. Thus a bound only on that occupancy distribution can- 23
24                                                                                                          24
     not be substituted for (13). The same example shows why changing the supremum
25                                                                                                          25
     in (15) to the transition of π is generally invalid. Weighted sampling-norm results
26                                                                                                          26
     require their own distribution-shift or coverage assumptions. We make no such
27                                                                                                          27
     inference from the finite query banks.

23                   S.34.1. Optimal-action intervals and comparative statics                                      23

24     The economic bands in Table XV use more information than a mean value-loss                                  24

25   certificate. Let Q be continuously differentiable and κ-strongly concave on [ℓ, u],                           25

26   with unique maximizer a∗ . For feasible a, let r ( a) be the directional residual in                          26

27   Proposition 4. Then                                                                                           27

28                                                                                                                 28
                                                   | a − a∗ | ≤ r ( a)/κ.                                (S.121)
29                                                                                                                 29

30   To see this for a < a∗ , the optimality condition gives Q′ ( a∗ ) ≥ 0 when a∗ = u, and                        30

31   gives zero at an interior optimum. Strong concavity then implies Q′ ( a) ≥ κ ( a∗ − a). 31
32   For a > a∗ , the reverse argument gives − Q′ ( a) ≥ κ ( a − a∗ ). At an endpoint the                          32
                                 NEURAL BELLMAN OPERATORS                               223

1    positive-part residual gives exactly the appropriate one-sided inequality. The case       1

2    a = a∗ is immediate.                                                                      2

3      Use the interval upper bound ri and the strictly positive curvature lower bound         3

4    κ i for each task. Outward arithmetic and intersection with feasibility give              4

5                                                                                            5
                                     ri     ri
6                          Ii = ai − , ai +      ∩ [ℓi , ui ], ai∗ ∈ Ii .                      6
                                     κi     κi
7                                                                                              7
     For the same tasks under a changed future θ and the anchor, the mean optimal
8                                                                                              8
     response belongs to q−1 ∑i ( Iθ,i − I0,i ). No independent-noise assumption is needed:
9                                                                                              9
     these are deterministic inclusions for fixed finite laws. We use the final NBO actions,
10                                                                                             10
     not the enumeration actions, to obtain the NBO response bands. The envelope over
11                                                                                             11
     three fitting streams contains every corresponding inclusion; it does not turn three
12                                                                                             12
     fixed streams into a population confidence interval. Printed endpoints are rounded
13                                                                                             13
     outwards. A negative upper endpoint establishes a negative mean optimal response
14                                                                                             14
     in that declared economy.

                              S.34.2. Source and arithmetic audit
17                                                                                             17

18     The R21 audit reads every original R20 service record, verifies its stored SHA256       18

19   digest, reestablishes the inherited source identities, regenerates only the fixed task    19

20   arguments, and recomputes the certificates at the saved actions. It does not retrain      20

21   any predictor or replace any clock. All 984 attempted certificates and 120 additional     21

22   zero-charge certificates are compared field for field with their original values. The     22

23   attempted checks cover 319,062 task actions. The audit also verifies feasibility,         23

24   stopping order, recorded success flags, every cost decomposition, and the exact           24

25   binary scaling used in the interval exponential implementation. This is an arithmetic     25

26   and source audit of the specified finite model, not an empirical assessment of            26

27   external economic calibration.                                                            27
